title: Oversight Without a Bottleneck: AI Control Applied to Improvement Loops

questions.question: When AI control is applied to a self-improvement loop, which assignment of the U / T / H roles is the one this lesson uses?
options: U is the frozen monitor scoring edits, T is the improver proposing them, H is the loop's own evaluator
U is the improver proposing edits, T is a frozen monitor scoring their suspiciousness, H is the human audit budget
U is the human reviewer reading edits, T is the improver proposing them, H is the archive of committed edits
U is the loop's internal evaluator, T is the archive of edits, H is the trusted model that rewrites edits
questions.explanation: The improver is the untrusted strong model U; the monitor must sit outside the loop so it cannot be improved into complicity, which makes it T; the scarce human labour is H.

questions.question: How is the audit threshold set in trusted monitoring, and why does that choice matter for the improver?
options: On the scores of a labelled set of harmful edits, so that each harmful edit scores above it and is always routed to a human for review
On the improver's own reported gain for each edit, so the edits claiming the largest improvements are the ones a human sees first
On the human's available hours in each cycle, so the number of audits is fixed in advance and the improver can plan around the schedule
On the distribution of benign edits' scores, so a benign edit is audited with probability b and the improver cannot tell which edits will be seen
questions.explanation: The paper calibrates at a 2% false-positive rate on honest solutions; because every edit faces the same noisy monitor and the same threshold, the improver has no channel it can buy its way into.

questions.question: In the default simulation (AUC 0.8, 5% audit budget, 2% attack rate, 160 edits per run) trusted monitoring reaches about 36% safety. Which calculation explains that number?
options: Safety is about 0.98^160 + (1 - 0.98^160) x P(harmful score > tau), i.e. 0.039 + 0.961 x 0.325, because the run is safe only if there is no harm or the first harmful edit is caught
Safety is about 0.05 x 160 / 20, i.e. 0.4, because the 5% audit budget is spread over 160 edits and 20 cycles, so roughly 40% of the cycles receive at least one human audit
Safety is about AUC x (1 - attack rate) x (1 - audit budget), i.e. 0.8 x 0.98 x 0.95, discounted by half because the attacker is allowed to choose where to place the harm
Safety is about 1 - (1 - 0.325)^3.2, i.e. 0.72, because 3.2 harmful edits are expected per run and each one is caught independently with probability 32.5%
questions.explanation: With d' = 1.19 and tau = 1.645 a harmful edit is caught with probability 32.5%; since the first committed harmful edit ends the run, safety is the chance of no harm plus the chance the first harmful edit is audited.

questions.question: Why does the inter-cycle pause rule still help against the adaptive attacker when trusted monitoring alone collapses to a few percent?
options: Because a pause resets the audit threshold to zero for the following cycle, so every edit the attacker proposes next is read by a human regardless of its score
Because the pause rule brings in a second copy of the improver to score the staged edits, and two copies of the same model cannot coordinate within one cycle
Because the adaptive attacker fools the per-edit monitor score, but a harmful edit still inflates the cycle's reported gain, which is an independent signal the rule watches
Because a pause gives the human time to retrain the monitor on the attacker's most recent edits, which restores the AUC before the next cycle starts
questions.explanation: The attacker optimises against the monitor's score, not against the gain-jump trigger; with seed 3 the monitor alone gives 4.7% safety and monitor plus pause gives 28.3%.

questions.question: A lab proposes: 'our researcher reads every edit the improver proposes before it is merged, so no monitor is needed.' What is this lesson's assessment?
options: It is the safest design available, since a perfect human reading everything dominates every sampled protocol on both safety and usefulness
It is acceptable as long as the researcher is senior, signs each approval, and the improver supplies a short summary of each edit to speed the reading
It works only if the improver is also asked to flag which of its own edits are risky, so the researcher can concentrate on those edits first
It is a bottleneck that degrades into a rubber stamp as volume grows; the protocol should keep the human sample small and let a trusted monitor score everything
questions.explanation: Reading everything either slows the loop to the human's pace or stops being reading; control keeps the human as the anchor by giving them a protocol-chosen sample, never a summary chosen by the improver.

questions.question: Which failure is a per-edit monitor structurally unable to catch, and what does the lesson propose instead?
options: A single edit that removes the sandbox's egress rule in one step; addressed by raising the audit budget until the monitor's recall reaches 100%
Harm distributed across many individually innocuous edits (slow drift); addressed by trajectory-level anchor metrics and the pause rule's gap trigger
An edit whose reported gain is obviously inflated relative to its peers; addressed by narrowing the defer band so that T replaces fewer benign edits
A harmful edit that a human auditor misread under time pressure; addressed by trusted editing, which lets T rewrite the edit the human approved
questions.explanation: A monitor scores one edit at a time, so harm that only exists across cycles never appears in any single score; the defences have to look at the trajectory, as Lesson 17's anchor metrics and the pause spec's gap threshold do.
